splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether possessing any one of the criteria is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on which circuit they are in.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps Auer/Kisor deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal provisions, including Sentencing Guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpreting the Guidelines in criminal sentencing. This matters because it determines whether ambiguity in criminal sentencing provisions is resolved in favor of the defendant or in favor of the government's preferred interpretation.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Chevron-type deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, meaning ambiguity must be resolved in favor of the defendant.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference applies even in criminal contexts, and that ambiguous Guidelines commentary may be given controlling weight over the rule of lenity.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses such as conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses like conspiracy to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects whether many defendants qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is valid and controlling
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the Guidelines that validly includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses within the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' and is entitled to deference under Stinson.

positions.label: Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 cannot expand the definition beyond its plain text, particularly under Kisor's narrowing of deference doctrines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute covers substances not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' is limited to substances controlled under federal law, or whether it encompasses state-law drug offenses even when the underlying substance is not federally controlled. The outcome significantly affects sentencing ranges for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-only substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law, without requiring the substance to also be controlled under federal law, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Must be federally controlled substance
positions.summary: Holds that a prior conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if it involves a substance also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, applying a categorical approach aligned with federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to good-faith debtors upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in asset value that occurs between the initial Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This split affects whether debtors who convert in good faith risk losing equity gains accrued during the Chapter 13 period.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A), read together with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, means that post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor rather than the estate, consistent with the statute's structure, legislative history, and policy of encouraging good-faith Chapter 13 filings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus or may proceed under civil rights statutes like Bivens or 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or whether civil rights actions are also available. The Supreme Court noted but left this question open in Preiser v. Rodriguez, and circuits have taken divergent approaches, particularly regarding BOP decisions on matters like First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus may be used to challenge conditions or terms of confinement, not just the fact or duration of imprisonment, giving prisoners broader access to habeas relief for BOP decisions.

positions.label: Habeas limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, and prisoners must use civil rights remedies for conditions-of-confinement claims.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while others allow courts to consider them, particularly following the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly in combination with other factors, and especially under the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must focus solely on reentry and rehabilitation goals.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether sentencing courts may impose punishment as a purpose of revocation of supervised release, or whether the goals of supervised release revocation are limited to promoting reentry and deterring future violations. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis permits express punishment, placing it at odds with other circuits.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions at revocation proceedings.

positions.label: Revocation must focus on reentry, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is to facilitate reentry and that punishment for the underlying violation is not a proper sentencing purpose at revocation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the deadline to appeal a Hyde Amendment ruling (attorney's fees in criminal cases) is governed by the civil appeal timeline (30 days) or the criminal appeal timeline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil deadline) or part of the criminal proceeding (subject to the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal proceeding and subject to the shorter criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on the timing constraints for actuarial assumptions used in calculating employer withdrawal liability under ERISA's multiemployer pension provisions. This split affected billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), not selected after the fact.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, as long as the assumptions themselves reflect the conditions as of that date.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects revocation proceedings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, so the supervision period is extended and courts retain jurisdiction to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: No tolling — term runs continuously
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms run continuously and are not tolled during absconding because there is no statutory authorization for the judicially-created fugitive tolling doctrine in this context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face Section 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on raising previously presented claims when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners are absolutely barred from re-raising any prior claim; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim that was presented in a prior motion.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, and such prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own gatekeeping requirements for successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures and ballot-counting rules. This split affects the ability of candidates to challenge election administration practices before an election takes place, with some circuits granting broader standing and others requiring more concrete injury.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge state election laws that affect ballot counting procedures, because the candidate faces competitive injury from potentially unlawful vote dilution.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate does not have Article III standing to challenge state ballot-receipt deadlines absent a concrete, particularized injury, finding the alleged competitive harm too speculative.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order effectively unreviewable after final judgment.
splits.description: Circuits have taken different approaches to whether denial of a motion to seal medical information qualifies for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy constitutes a 'value of high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have been more restrictive about applying the collateral order doctrine to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses involves a value of 'high order' that is effectively unreviewable after final judgment, making it immediately appealable.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the interest in sealing can be adequately vindicated through post-judgment appeal or other means.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination claims in hospitality settings, indicating that lower courts have applied divergent standards. The decision could affect hospitality, retail, and service industries nationwide by establishing clearer rules for fair treatment and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies broader standards for proving discrimination in places of public accommodation, potentially lowering the threshold for establishing liability.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims against business operators, requiring stronger showings of intentional or systemic discrimination.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
